title: Musculoskeletal Embryology
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the musculoskeletal system from the embryo to the adult layout. It covers how somites build the vertebrae, ribs, back muscles, and dermis; why each vertebral body is assembled from two sclerotome halves; how signaling centers shape the limb bud; why the limbs rotate in opposite directions; how bone forms by intramembranous and endochondral ossification; and how joints and pharyngeal arch muscles arise. Board questions rarely ask for a date alone. They give an adult finding, such as a nerve supply, a dermatome pattern, a short-limbed skeleton, or an extra digit, and ask you to work back to the embryonic step that explains it.
prerequisites: Gastrulation and the three germ layers, including paraxial, intermediate, and lateral plate mesoderm
Notochord and neural tube formation and the role of sonic hedgehog in the neural tube
Basic structure of a spinal nerve: roots, dorsal and ventral rami
Hyaline cartilage and bone histology: chondrocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, osteoid
Signaling families: FGF, Wnt, hedgehog, BMP, and HOX transcription factors

connections.how: Resegmentation explains why spinal nerves exit at disc level and why there are eight cervical nerves but seven cervical vertebrae.
Limb rotation and the dorsal and ventral muscle masses predict which nerve supplies each compartment and why the lower limb dermatomes spiral.

connections.to: Bone physiology and metabolic bone disease
connections.how: The growth plate built during endochondral ossification is the site affected in achondroplasia and in disorders of linear growth.

connections.to: Head and neck anatomy and the cranial nerves
connections.how: The pharyngeal arch of origin predicts the motor nerve of each muscle of mastication, facial expression, pharynx, and larynx.
Thalidomide, HOX mutations, FGFR3 mutation, and RUNX2 loss show how a single signal or gene produces a predictable skeletal defect.

terms.def: A paired, segmental block of paraxial mesoderm beside the neural tube that forms sclerotome, myotome, and dermatome.
The ventromedial part of a somite that migrates around the notochord and neural tube to form vertebrae and ribs.
The part of a somite that forms skeletal muscle; clinically, the group of muscles supplied by one spinal nerve segment.
Embryologically, the part of a somite that forms dermis of the back; clinically, the skin area supplied by one spinal nerve.
The dorsal (back muscle) and ventral (body wall and limb muscle) divisions of the myotome, supplied by dorsal and ventral rami.
Formation of each vertebral body from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next.
Thickened ectoderm at the distal rim of the limb bud whose FGFs drive proximal to distal outgrowth.
Posterior limb bud mesenchyme that secretes sonic hedgehog to pattern the anterior to posterior (thumb to little finger) axis.
The cranial border of the early limb bud, which carries the radius and thumb or the tibia and big toe.
Bone formation in which a hyaline cartilage model is formed first and then replaced by bone.
A band of dense mesenchyme between two cartilage models that forms a joint instead of cartilage.
A paired bar of mesenchyme in the embryonic neck that contains neural crest skeleton, muscle, an artery, and its own cranial nerve.

blocks.text: Somites are paired blocks of paraxial mesoderm that form on each side of the neural tube and notochord. The first pair appears in the future occipital region at about day 20, and new pairs bud off in a cranial to caudal order at about three pairs per day until the end of week 5, giving about 42 to 44 pairs. The caudal-most pairs later regress. Each boundary forms on a timer: a clock of oscillating Notch and Wnt signaling in the presomitic mesoderm meets a receding FGF gradient, and a new somite separates each time the two coincide. This periodic origin is why vertebrae, ribs, back muscles, and spinal nerves are segmental.

Each somite then divides according to signals from its neighbors. Sonic hedgehog (Shh) from the notochord and the floor plate of the neural tube induces the ventromedial part to become sclerotome, which expresses PAX1, loses its epithelial arrangement, and migrates around the notochord and neural tube. Wnt signals from the dorsal neural tube and surface ectoderm keep the dorsolateral part as dermomyotome, which expresses PAX3 and gives rise to the myotome, the source of skeletal muscle, and the dermatome, the source of the dermis of the back.

blocks.title: From paraxial mesoderm to adult derivatives
steps: Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites from about day 20
Notochord and floor plate Shh induce ventromedial sclerotome
Sclerotome surrounds notochord and neural tube: vertebrae, ribs
Dorsal neural tube Wnt maintains dorsolateral dermomyotome
Dermomyotome forms myotome (muscle) and dermatome (back dermis)
Myotome splits into epaxial and hypaxial divisions
blocks.caption: Signals from the notochord and neural tube decide which part of each somite becomes skeleton, muscle, or dermis.

blocks.text: Muscle keeps the nerve of the segment it came from. Each spinal nerve divides into a dorsal ramus, which enters the epaxial (dorsomedial) muscle mass, and a ventral ramus, which follows the hypaxial (ventrolateral) mass into the body wall and limbs. Epaxial muscle becomes the deep, intrinsic back muscles such as erector spinae and transversospinalis. Hypaxial muscle becomes the intercostal and abdominal wall muscles, the prevertebral and scalene muscles, and, after its precursor cells migrate into the limb buds, all limb muscle. The limb bones, tendons, and connective tissue come instead from lateral plate mesoderm.

This explains a classic distinction. The superficial muscles on the back, such as trapezius, latissimus dorsi, and the rhomboids, are not epaxial; they migrated onto the back and are supplied by ventral rami of the brachial plexus or, for trapezius, by the accessory nerve. Only the deep muscles of the vertebral column are supplied by dorsal rami. Because segmental innervation is kept, injury to one spinal nerve produces a predictable band of sensory loss (its dermatome) and weakness of a predictable muscle group (its myotome).

blocks.title: Somite parts, adult derivatives, and nerve supply
rows: Vertebral bodies and arches, ribs, annulus fibrosus, part of the occipital bone
Dermis of the skin of the neck and back
Deep back muscles: erector spinae, transversospinalis, splenius, suboccipital
Limb, intercostal, abdominal wall, scalene, prevertebral, and infrahyoid muscles
blocks.caption: Limb dermis, bone, and tendon are not somite derivatives; they come from lateral plate mesoderm.

blocks.text: Sclerotome cells that surround the notochord form the vertebral bodies, those that surround the neural tube form the vertebral arches, and in the thoracic region the costal processes grow out to become ribs. A vertebra does not come from a single sclerotome. Each sclerotome splits into a loosely packed cranial half and a densely packed caudal half, and the caudal half of one sclerotome fuses with the cranial half of the next to form one vertebral body. This is resegmentation. Cells at the junction between the two original halves do not join either body; they fill the space between adjacent bodies and form the annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc.

Resegmentation solves a mechanical problem. The myotomes do not shift, so after resegmentation each muscle segment attaches to two adjacent vertebrae and crosses the disc between them, which is what allows segmental muscles to move the spine. For the same reason the spinal nerve, which grew toward its own myotome, now lies at the level of the disc and leaves through the intervertebral foramen, and the intersegmental arteries, which ran between somites, now cross the middle of each vertebral body.

blocks.title: Resegmentation of the sclerotomes
steps: Sclerotome cells surround the notochord and neural tube
Each sclerotome splits into loose cranial and dense caudal halves
Caudal half fuses with the next cranial half: one vertebral body
Cells between the original halves form the annulus fibrosus
Notochord regresses in bodies, persists between them as nucleus pulposus
Myotomes now span discs; spinal nerves lie at disc level
blocks.caption: Vertebrae end up offset by half a segment from the myotomes and spinal nerves.

blocks.text: The same shift explains spinal nerve numbering. The cranial half of the first cervical sclerotome fuses with the caudal half of the last occipital sclerotome and is incorporated into the occipital bone, so the first cervical nerve emerges between the skull and the atlas. There are therefore eight cervical nerves but seven cervical vertebrae: nerves C1 to C7 exit above the vertebra of the same number, C8 exits between C7 and T1, and from T1 downward each nerve exits below its numbered vertebra.

The notochord is squeezed out of the developing vertebral bodies, where it regresses, but persists and expands between them as the gelatinous nucleus pulposus, which the annulus fibrosus then encircles. The large notochordal cells largely disappear from the nucleus during childhood and are replaced by smaller chondrocyte-like cells. Notochordal rests left along the axis, most often in the sacrococcygeal region and the clivus at the skull base, can give rise to chordoma, a slow-growing malignant tumor of vacuolated (physaliferous) cells that express brachyury, a notochordal transcription factor.

blocks.title: Errors of vertebral development
rows: One lateral half of a vertebral body fails to form
Fused cervical vertebrae, short neck, low posterior hairline, limited neck motion
Vertebral arches fail to fuse dorsally, usually at L5 or S1
Skin-covered defect, sometimes a tuft of hair; cord usually normal
May compress the lower brachial plexus or subclavian artery
Malignant tumor of the clivus or sacrum
blocks.caption: Each defect traces to one step: somite segmentation, sclerotome growth, arch fusion, costal process growth, or notochord regression.

blocks.predict: A fetal ultrasound shows a hemivertebra at T8 in which only the left half of the body formed. Which way will the spine curve?
blocks.explain: The left side of that segment has a vertebral half and the right side has none, so the left side is taller. The spine bends away from the taller side, producing a scoliosis convex to the left at that level, and the curve tends to worsen with growth because the left half keeps growing.

sections.title: Limb bud signaling and limb defects

blocks.text: Limb buds appear near the end of week 4 as outpocketings of the ventrolateral body wall, the upper limb first and the lower limb one to two days later. Each bud is a core of mesenchyme from the somatic layer of lateral plate mesoderm covered by surface ectoderm. Three signaling centers pattern its three axes, and HOX genes give each segment its identity.

At the distal rim, mesenchymal FGF10 induces the ectoderm to thicken into the apical ectodermal ridge (AER). The AER secretes FGFs, including FGF8 and FGF4, that keep the mesenchyme beneath it (the progress zone) dividing and undifferentiated. In the classic model, cells that leave this zone early form proximal structures and cells that leave late form distal ones, so the limb is laid down proximal to distal: arm or thigh, then forearm or leg, then hand or foot. Loss of the AER stops outgrowth, giving amelia (absent limb) or meromelia (partial absence).

The zone of polarizing activity (ZPA), mesenchyme at the posterior (postaxial) border, secretes sonic hedgehog (Shh). Digit identity depends on how much Shh a cell receives and for how long: the little finger side receives the most, and the thumb forms without it. If Shh is also made at the anterior border, by a graft or by mutation of its limb enhancer (the ZRS), a second gradient produces extra anterior digits: preaxial polydactyly, sometimes a mirror-image duplication. The AER and ZPA sustain each other, which couples growth to pattern. The third center, WNT7A in the dorsal ectoderm, induces LMX1B in dorsal mesenchyme to make dorsal structures; LMX1B mutation causes nail-patella syndrome, with small or absent nails and patellae.

blocks.title: The AER and ZPA maintain each other
steps: AER FGFs maintain Shh expression in the ZPA
ZPA Shh induces the BMP antagonist gremlin in mesenchyme
Gremlin blocks BMP, which would shut down the AER
AER keeps secreting FGFs, maintaining Shh
blocks.caption: The loop ends as the bud grows and gremlin falls, so outgrowth and patterning stop together.

blocks.text: HOX genes are transcription factors expressed in nested domains along the limb. Genes at the 5 prime end of the HOXA and HOXD clusters (paralog groups 9 to 13) switch on progressively later and more distally, and HOX13 genes mark the hand and foot. HOXD13 mutation causes synpolydactyly, with fused digits and an extra digit in the web, and HOXA13 mutation causes hand-foot-genital syndrome. Digits separate by BMP-driven apoptosis between them; failure gives syndactyly.

Thalidomide shows that timing decides the defect. Exposure while the limb buds form and grow out, about days 24 to 36 after fertilization, causes limb reduction defects, most characteristically phocomelia, in which the hands or feet attach close to the trunk because the long bones are absent or rudimentary. The leading explanation is that thalidomide binds cereblon, part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase, redirecting it to degrade transcription factors such as SALL4 that limb outgrowth needs. Later exposure spares the limbs.

blocks.title: Limb signaling centers and their defects
blocks.caption: Name the abnormal axis to find the responsible center and signal.

blocks.predict: In a chick embryo, the AER is removed once early in outgrowth and, in a second embryo, late in outgrowth. How will the two limbs differ?
blocks.explain: Early removal leaves only proximal structures, because outgrowth stops before the forearm and hand are laid down. Late removal loses only the most distal elements, such as the digits, because proximal segments were already laid down.
blocks.check: The AER paragraph and the proximal to distal sequence.

blocks.text: Both limb buds start with the same layout. The cranial border is the preaxial border, which will carry the radius and thumb in the arm and the tibia and big toe in the leg; the caudal border is postaxial. Myoblasts gather into a dorsal muscle mass, which forms the extensors and is supplied by posterior division nerves of the plexus, and a ventral mass, which forms the flexors (and thigh adductors) and is supplied by anterior division nerves. Dermatomes run in segmental order, cranial segments preaxial and caudal segments postaxial.

In weeks 7 and 8 the limbs bend at the elbow and knee and rotate about their long axes in opposite directions. The upper limb rotates about 90 degrees laterally, so the elbow points backward, the extensors lie posteriorly, and the thumb lies laterally. The lower limb rotates about 90 degrees medially, so the knee points forward, the extensors lie anteriorly, the flexors posteriorly, and the big toe medially. The palm and the sole are therefore both ventral, flexor surfaces. Its cellular cause is not fully understood, but the result suits each limb's job: lateral rotation turns the palms forward for grasping, and medial rotation puts the knee extensors in front to straighten and lock the knee for weight bearing, with the sole on the ground.

Because muscles and nerves keep their embryonic surface, rotation predicts compartment and nerve. Posterior division nerves (axillary and radial in the arm; femoral, superior and inferior gluteal, and common fibular in the leg) supply the original dorsal, extensor surface, which is now the back of the arm but the front of the thigh and leg. Anterior division nerves (musculocutaneous, median, and ulnar; obturator and tibial) supply the original ventral surface, now the front of the arm but the medial and posterior thigh and the back of the leg. Dorsiflexion of the ankle is an extensor action, so it is performed by anterior leg muscles.

Dermatomes are mapped before rotation, so rotation twists them. In the upper limb the pattern stays readable: C5 and C6 run along the lateral (preaxial) side to the thumb, C7 reaches the middle finger, and C8 and T1 run along the medial (postaxial) side. In the lower limb, medial rotation carries the preaxial strip around to the front and medial side, so the bands run obliquely downward and medially in a spiral: L1 near the inguinal ligament, L2 and L3 over the anterior thigh, L4 over the knee and medial leg, L5 over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, S1 over the lateral border and sole of the foot, and S2 up the back of the leg and thigh.

blocks.title: Opposite rotations of the upper and lower limb
rows: C5, C6 on the lateral side
blocks.caption: Find the embryonic surface first, then apply the rotation.

blocks.title: Predicting compartment and nerve from rotation
blocks.text: Where should quadriceps lie, and which nerve supplies it? It extends the knee, so it is a dorsal mass muscle supplied by a posterior division nerve: femoral, L2 to L4. Medial rotation carried the dorsal surface forward, so quadriceps lies anteriorly. Triceps is also dorsal mass and posterior division (radial), but lateral rotation left the dorsal surface behind, so it lies posteriorly. The hamstrings flex the knee, so they are ventral mass muscles supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (anterior divisions) and lie posteriorly. The one exception, the short head of biceps femoris, is supplied by the common fibular division.

Bone forms by two routes, and the route decides which bones a disorder affects. In intramembranous ossification, mesenchymal cells condense, switch on the transcription factor RUNX2, and differentiate directly into osteoblasts that secrete osteoid, which then mineralizes. Woven bone spicules join into trabeculae, later remodeled into compact plates. This route builds the flat bones of the skull vault, most facial bones, much of the mandible, and most of the clavicle, the first bone to begin ossifying at about weeks 5 to 6. Skull bones grow at their edges, so the sutures and fontanelles let the vault enlarge with the brain.

In endochondral ossification, mesenchyme condenses and, under SOX9, forms a hyaline cartilage model covered by perichondrium. A cartilage model can grow from within by chondrocyte division, which bone cannot, so long bones, vertebrae, ribs, the pelvis, and the skull base use this route. The primary ossification center forms in the diaphysis, and by about week 12 primary centers are present in all the long bones of the limbs. Secondary centers appear in the epiphyses, mostly after birth; the distal femoral center is usually present at term. Between them, the epiphyseal growth plate keeps producing cartilage that is replaced from the diaphyseal side, lengthening the bone until the plates close after puberty under the influence of estrogen.

blocks.title: Endochondral ossification of a long bone
steps: Mesenchyme forms a hyaline cartilage model with perichondrium
Midshaft perichondrium becomes periosteum and lays a bone collar
Central chondrocytes hypertrophy, calcify matrix, release VEGF, and die
Periosteal bud vessels bring osteoprogenitors and osteoclast precursors
Primary ossification center forms in the diaphysis
Secondary centers form in the epiphyses, mostly after birth
Growth plates lengthen the bone, then close after puberty
blocks.caption: Cartilage is not turned into bone; calcified cartilage is removed and bone replaces it.

blocks.text: Growth plate chondrocytes are held in balance by a feedback loop in which Indian hedgehog from prehypertrophic chondrocytes stimulates PTHrP near the bone ends, and PTHrP keeps chondrocytes dividing and delays their hypertrophy. FGFR3 signaling restrains chondrocyte proliferation. A disorder acting mainly on one route shows mainly in its bones, which makes the skeletal pattern diagnostic (see the STOP below).

blocks.title: Intramembranous versus endochondral ossification
rows: Skull vault, facial bones, most of clavicle
Long bones, vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, skull base
blocks.caption: RUNX2 is needed for osteoblasts in both routes, but its loss shows most clearly in intramembranous bones.

blocks.text: Joints form at interzones, bands of dense mesenchyme between adjacent cartilage models, from about week 6, and by the end of week 8 they resemble adult joints. Interzone cells express GDF5 and make no cartilage. Where the interzone becomes dense fibrous tissue, a fibrous joint forms, such as a suture; where it becomes cartilage, a cartilaginous joint forms, such as the pubic symphysis. In a synovial joint the central interzone cavitates, through cell death and hyaluronan secretion, to form the joint cavity, while the surrounding mesenchyme forms the capsule, synovial membrane, and ligaments, and intra-articular structures such as menisci also arise from the interzone. Cavitation depends on fetal movement, so disorders that immobilize the fetus leave stiff joints at birth (arthrogryposis).

blocks.predict: One child has absent clavicles, a wide anterior fontanelle, and extra teeth. Another has short arms and legs, a large skull vault with a flat midface, and a near-normal trunk length. Which ossification route fails in each?
blocks.explain: The first has cleidocranial dysplasia: loss of one RUNX2 copy impairs osteoblast formation, most visibly in intramembranous bones. The second has achondroplasia: gain-of-function FGFR3 slows growth plate proliferation, so endochondral long bones and skull base are short while the intramembranous vault grows normally.

sections.title: Pharyngeal arch muscles and their nerves

blocks.text: The pharyngeal arches are paired bars of mesenchyme that appear in weeks 4 and 5 on each side of the developing head and neck, separated externally by clefts and internally by pouches. Arches 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6 develop in humans; the fifth is absent or rudimentary. Each arch is covered by ectoderm outside and endoderm inside and contains four components: a skeletal element and connective tissue from neural crest, an aortic arch artery, muscle from cranial paraxial mesoderm, and a cranial nerve that grows in from the adjacent hindbrain.

Each arch's muscle is supplied by the nerve of its own arch and keeps that nerve wherever it migrates, just as somite muscle keeps its spinal nerve. Temporalis spreads up to the temple and the facial muscles spread over the scalp and down the neck as platysma, yet they remain supplied by the nerves of arches 1 and 2. The arch nerves run V3, VII, IX, X, so the motor nerve of a head or neck muscle follows from its arch (table). The fourth arch is supplied by the superior laryngeal and pharyngeal branches of the vagus, and the sixth by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The right recurrent nerve hooks under the subclavian artery (fourth arch artery) and the left under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum (sixth arch artery), because the distal right sixth arch artery regresses.

blocks.title: Pharyngeal arch muscles, nerves, and lesion signs
rows: Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini
Weak chewing; jaw deviates toward the lesion on opening
Muscles of facial expression, buccinator, platysma, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric
Facial paralysis; hyperacusis from stapedius loss
Weak elevation of the pharynx, rarely detectable alone
Pharyngeal constrictors, cricothyroid, levator veli palatini, palatoglossus
CN X (superior laryngeal and pharyngeal branches)
Dysphagia; uvula deviates away from the lesion; loss of high pitch with cricothyroid palsy
blocks.caption: Arches 1, 2, and 3 use nerves V3, VII, and IX; arches 4 and 6 both use the vagus.

blocks.text: Lesion signs follow the muscle actions. With a V3 lesion, the intact lateral pterygoid pulls its condyle forward unopposed, so the jaw deviates toward the weak side. With a VII lesion, stapedius no longer damps ossicle movement, so sounds seem too loud. With a vagal lesion, the intact levator veli palatini pulls the uvula away from the lesion. Cricothyroid tilts the thyroid cartilage to lengthen and tense the vocal folds, so its loss lowers vocal pitch range, while the sixth arch muscles open, close, and adjust the folds, so recurrent nerve injury causes hoarseness.

Two exceptions are often tested. The tongue muscles, except palatoglossus, come from occipital somites and are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not an arch nerve. Stylopharyngeus is the only third arch muscle and is a longitudinal elevator, whereas the constrictors belong to the fourth arch and the vagus.

blocks.title: Localizing a lesion with the arch map
blocks.text: A man cannot close his left eye or raise the left corner of his mouth, and loud sounds hurt his left ear. Chewing and jaw opening are normal, and his uvula is midline. Facial expression muscles and stapedius are second arch muscles, so the lesion is the left facial nerve, CN VII, proximal to the branch to stapedius in the facial canal. Normal chewing and jaw opening exclude a first arch (V3) lesion, and a midline uvula excludes a vagal (fourth arch) lesion. The posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid are also second arch muscles, but their weakness is rarely noticed clinically.

integration.text: One rule ties this chapter together: a muscle keeps the nerve of the segment or arch where it formed, however far it migrates. Somite muscle keeps its spinal nerve and divides into epaxial (dorsal ramus) and hypaxial (ventral ramus) territories; limb muscle keeps the posterior or anterior division nerve of its dorsal or ventral mass even after rotation turns that surface to the front or back; and arch muscle keeps V3, VII, IX, or X. Clinical dermatome and myotome maps, the anterior thigh extensors, the medial big toe, and the vagal supply of the larynx all follow from this rule plus the movements of development.

Molecular biology and pathology explain the defects. A single signal or gene acting at one step gives a predictable lesion: FGF from the AER for limb length, Shh from the ZPA for digit pattern, LMX1B for dorsal structures, HOXD13 and HOXA13 for distal identity, FGFR3 for growth plate proliferation, and RUNX2 for osteoblasts. Teratogens such as thalidomide act only during the window when their target step is underway. Three limits apply: timing figures are approximate and differ among texts, the progress zone model of limb outgrowth is a simplification still debated, and the cause of limb rotation is described better than it is explained.

summary: Somites form from paraxial mesoderm from about day 20; Shh from notochord and floor plate makes sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), and Wnt maintains dermomyotome (myotome and back dermis).
Epaxial myotome forms the deep back muscles supplied by dorsal rami; hypaxial myotome forms body wall and limb muscles supplied by ventral rami; limb bone and tendon come from lateral plate mesoderm.

Each vertebral body forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next, so myotomes span discs, nerves exit at disc level, and there are eight cervical nerves but seven cervical vertebrae.
The notochord persists as the nucleus pulposus; its rests can form chordoma in the clivus or sacrum.
AER FGFs drive proximal to distal outgrowth; ZPA Shh sets digit identity, and ectopic anterior Shh causes preaxial polydactyly; WNT7A and LMX1B set the dorsal side; HOX genes set segment identity.
Thalidomide during limb outgrowth (about days 24 to 36) causes phocomelia.

The upper limb rotates laterally and the lower limb medially, so extensors are posterior in the arm and anterior in the thigh and leg, the thumb is lateral and the big toe medial, and lower limb dermatomes spiral.
Intramembranous ossification (skull vault, most of the clavicle) needs RUNX2 and no cartilage; endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model and lengthens bone at growth plates.
Joints form from interzone mesenchyme; synovial cavities form by cavitation, which requires fetal movement.
Arch muscles keep their nerves: first V3 (mastication), second VII (facial expression), third IX (stylopharyngeus), fourth and sixth X (pharynx and larynx).

verify: Timing figures vary among texts: first somites about day 20, total somite pairs about 42 to 44, limb buds near the end of week 4 (upper limb about day 24 to 26, lower a day or two later), and rotation in week 7 or weeks 7 to 8. Confirm the values NABNE expects.

The thalidomide window for limb defects is quoted as about days 24 to 36 after fertilization here; other sources give days 20 to 36 for all thalidomide embryopathy or narrower ranges for upper and lower limbs.
The cereblon and SALL4 mechanism of thalidomide limb defects is the current leading explanation; anti-angiogenic and oxidative stress mechanisms are also proposed.
Newer editions of Langman describe primaxial and abaxial muscle domains alongside the traditional epaxial and hypaxial terms; confirm which terminology NABNE uses.

The fate of notochordal cells in the adult nucleus pulposus (replacement versus differentiation into chondrocyte-like cells) is debated; the chapter states only that the large notochordal cells largely disappear in childhood.
The exact segment of the occipital sclerotome that fuses with the first cervical sclerotome is given as the fourth occipital in Langman; this chapter says the last occipital sclerotome.
Lower limb dermatome boundaries (for example whether the big toe is L4 or L5) differ among dermatome maps.
Requested new diagram names for a future revision: somite-cross-section (neural tube, notochord, sclerotome, dermomyotome, dorsal and ventral rami) and limb-bud-axes (AER, ZPA, dorsal ectoderm).
